title: Industrial control system and OT security
summary: How plants are controlled (PLCs, ladder logic, SCADA, safety systems), why Modbus and DNP3 trust everyone, what Stuxnet, Ukraine, Triton and Colonial taught, and how OT is segmented, watched and recovered.
outcomes: Explain how OT differs from IT: safety and availability first, real-time loops, long lifetimes and planned patch windows
Name the parts of a control system (sensor, actuator, PLC, RTU, HMI, historian, SIS) and place them in the Purdue model
Decode a Modbus/TCP frame by hand and in Python, and explain why classic industrial protocols lack authentication
Describe at concept level how setpoint changes and spoofed HMI views attack a process, and how independent safety systems limit them

lessons.title: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT

blocks.md:
Most of security is about **information technology (IT)**: computers that store and move data. This course is about computers that move *things*. NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) defines **operational technology (OT)** as programmable systems and devices that "interact with the physical environment": they detect or cause a direct change in the physical world. The name contrasts the two: IT handles information, OT runs operations.

An **industrial control system (ICS)** is the best-known kind of OT: the computers that run power grids, water plants, pipelines, refineries and factories. NIST's guide to this field is [NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/82/r3/final) (SP means Special Publication). Its third revision, in 2023, widened the title from ICS to OT, because building automation, transport and physical access control systems share the same problems.

**Tiny example.** A water tank must stay between 200 and 300 cm. A sensor measures the level, a controller (here a **PLC**, programmable logic controller, lesson 3) compares it with those two **setpoints** (NIST: "an input variable that sets the desired value"), and a pump fills the tank when the level is low. NIST calls this a **control loop**: sensors, controllers and actuators that "manipulate some controlled process". If the output feeds back into the input, as here, it is a **closed loop**; NIST also names open loop (fixed settings) and manual mode (humans do everything). Operators watch the loop and set values on an **HMI** (human-machine interface, the screens and buttons people use).

We will reuse this tank through the whole course: its setpoints become Modbus registers, its logic becomes ladder logic, and its attack scenario shows why a lying screen is dangerous.

blocks.title: A control loop: measure, compare, act, repeat

nodes.label:
Actuator P-101
pump on or off

scenes.caption: The process is the physical thing being controlled: a tank whose level must stay between 200 and 300 cm. Water drains out at a steady 3 cm per minute because people downstream use it.
A sensor turns a physical property into a number. Level sensor LT-101 reports 195 cm to the controller.
The controller compares the measurement with its setpoints (desired values). 195 is below the low setpoint of 200, so it decides: start the pump.

The actuator turns a command into physical action: the pump adds 8 cm per minute, so the level rises 5 cm per minute net. The sensor sees the change on the next reading. That feedback is what makes the loop closed.
Humans supervise through the HMI: they read status and change setpoints. They do not switch the pump themselves; the controller does, many times a second if needed.
At 320 cm the level is at or above the 300 cm high setpoint, so the controller stops the pump and the level drains back. Whoever can change the setpoints or the measurement steers the water.

blocks.code:
# A closed control loop in miniature: one tank, one pump, one controller.
LOW_SP, HIGH_SP = 200, 300   # setpoints in cm, set by an operator on the HMI
FILL, DRAIN = 8, 3           # cm per minute: pump inflow, constant demand

level, pump = 210, False
for minute in range(0, 60, 5):
    # 1. sensor: the level transmitter measures the process
    measured = level
    # 2. controller: compare the measurement with the setpoints
    if measured < LOW_SP:
        pump = True
    elif measured >= HIGH_SP:
        pump = False
    # 3. actuator: the pump changes the process, which the sensor sees next time
    print(f"t={minute:2d} min  level={level:3d} cm  pump={'ON ' if pump else 'off'}")
    level += 5 * ((FILL if pump else 0) - DRAIN)
blocks.caption: Runnable Python. Output: the pump starts at t=5 (195 cm) and stops at t=30 (320 cm), then the level drains. Change HIGH_SP to 380 and rerun: the tank fills far higher with no other sign that anything changed.

blocks.md:
**Why OT security differs.** NIST SP 800-82r3 lists the special considerations:
- **Safety first.** In IT the main concerns are data confidentiality and integrity. In OT "human safety is paramount, followed by protection of the process", and "any security measure that impairs safety is unacceptable".
- **Availability.** Many processes run continuously; outages "must often be planned and scheduled days or weeks in advance". Rebooting, the IT cure-all, "may not be acceptable".
- **Real time.** OT is "time-critical"; delay and jitter (variation in delay) can be unacceptable, while high throughput is not essential.
- **Change management.** Patches must be tested by the vendor and the owner before use, and many OT systems run operating systems the vendor no longer supports.
- **Lifetime and location.** IT parts last about 3 to 5 years, OT parts about 10 to 15 "and sometimes longer", often at remote unstaffed sites.

blocks.title: Typical component lifetime in years (NIST SP 800-82r3)

scenes.caption: Lower end of NIST's ranges: IT parts are replaced after about 3 years, OT parts after about 10.
Upper end: about 5 years for IT and about 15 for OT, 'and sometimes longer'. A controller installed today may still run when today's laptops are long recycled.

blocks.md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.
IT protects data; OT protects people, equipment and the process. The order of priorities is different (safety and availability first), and every defence in this course is shaped by that.

blocks.question: A security analyst finds that a plant's HMI computer runs an operating system with no vendor patches. What does NIST's guidance suggest as the first response?
options: Work with control engineers to plan a tested change in a scheduled outage, and meanwhile add other protections (segmentation, letting only approved programs run, monitoring)
Leave it alone forever, since OT cannot change
Patch or reimage it tonight, as you would an office laptop
Unplug it immediately to remove the risk
blocks.explain: NIST notes OT updates must be tested and outages planned days or weeks ahead, and that unsupported operating systems are common. The answer is a planned change plus compensating controls. Unplugging the HMI may blind operators and is itself a safety and availability risk.

blocks.question: In the tank loop, which component turns a decision into a physical change?
options: The sensor
The HMI
The actuator (the pump)
The setpoint
blocks.explain: The actuator acts on the process. Sensors measure, the controller decides, the HMI lets humans supervise, and setpoints are the desired values the controller compares against.

lessons.title: Inside a plant: sensors, PLCs, RTUs, HMIs, historians and SIS

blocks.md:
Before we can defend a plant we need names for its parts. All definitions here come from NIST SP 800-82r3 and its glossary.

- **Sensor**: "produces a voltage or current output that is representative of some physical property" (speed, temperature, flow).
- **Actuator**: converts energy (electric, hydraulic, pneumatic) into motion; "the mechanism by which a control system acts upon an environment". Valves, breakers, switches and motors are actuators.
- **PLC (programmable logic controller)**: "a solid-state control system that has a user-programmable memory" for I/O control, logic, timing, counting and three-mode PID control (proportional-integral-derivative, a standard feedback algorithm). The name says what it replaced: logic that used to be wired in relays became a program (lesson 3).
- **RTU (remote terminal unit)**: a computer at a remote site, classically with radio links where wires are unavailable; PLCs with radios are often used instead.
- **IED (intelligent electronic device)**: a smart field device such as a **protective relay**, which trips a breaker when it sees a fault.

- **HMI (human-machine interface)**: "the hardware or software through which an operator interacts with a controller", from a panel of buttons and lights to a PC showing live graphics.
- **SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition)**: a system that gathers data and applies control "over long distances", such as grids and pipelines. The name lists its two jobs: supervise remote sites and acquire their data.
- **DCS (distributed control system)**: control "distributed about the process" rather than in one unit, typical inside one large plant such as a refinery.
- **Data historian**: a central database of process values over time, used for trends and analysis.
- **Engineering workstation**: the computer used to configure, program and diagnose controllers.
- **SIS (safety instrumented system)**: an independent system of sensors, logic solvers and final elements that brings the process "to a safe state when predetermined thresholds are violated". It is built to the standard IEC 61511 (IEC is the International Electrotechnical Commission). Lesson 11 is about an attack on one.

blocks.title: A SCADA system: control center and field sites (after NIST)

nodes.label:
WAN: radio, phone line,
cable or satellite

scenes.caption: Field sites first. Each has a controller wired to sensors and actuators: a PLC, an RTU (a remote unit built for long-distance links) or an IED such as a protective relay.
The control center talks to field sites over long, often shared links. NIST: SCADA was designed for the delays and data-integrity problems of phone lines, microwave and satellite.
The control server polls the field and runs alarms. Operators watch and command through the HMI; the historian stores every value for trends and reports.
The engineering workstation holds the PLC programs and the tools to change them. For an attacker it is the most valuable machine in the room; for a defender, the one to guard hardest.

blocks.md:
**Where they live.** A SCADA system has a control center (control server, HMI, engineering workstations, historian on a LAN) and field sites with RTUs, PLCs and IEDs. NIST notes that field sites "are often equipped with a remote access capability" for diagnostics, over a modem or WAN. A PLC-only system, such as one assembly line, may have no central server at all.

The **basic process control system (BPCS)**, NIST's term for the normal control layer, keeps the process on target. The SIS sits beside it and only acts when the BPCS has failed to keep things safe. NIST: an SIS is "often independent from all other control systems" so that a BPCS failure does not disable it.

blocks.md: Learn to read a plant by asking three questions of each box: what physical thing can it change, who can talk to it, and what would happen if it lied. Those three questions drive the rest of this course.

blocks.question: A refinery's safety system is designed so that it can still shut the unit down even if the main control system has crashed. Which design property is this?
options: Redundancy of the historian
Independence of the SIS from the BPCS
Real-time scheduling of the HMI
Remote access to field sites
blocks.explain: NIST describes the SIS as often independent from other control systems so that a BPCS failure does not harm SIS function. That independence is exactly what attackers in the Triton case worked to get around.

blocks.question: Which machine would an attacker most want in order to change a PLC's program, and so which deserves the strongest protection?
options: The data historian
A sensor
The HMI's display monitor
The engineering workstation
blocks.explain: The engineering workstation holds the programming software and project files and can download logic to controllers. Stuxnet and Triton both worked through such machines.

lessons.title: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic

blocks.md:
**Where PLCs came from.** Before PLCs, factory logic was built from relays: electrically operated switches wired together in big panels. Control Design's history of PLC programming notes that PLCs appeared "in the early 1970s" as "a replacement for hardwired relay logic panels". To keep electricians comfortable, the first programming language drew the program like the relay wiring diagram it replaced: **ladder logic**, named for its look of two vertical power rails joined by horizontal **rungs**.

The standard **IEC 61131-3** long defined five PLC languages: ladder diagram (LD), function block diagram (FBD), sequential function chart (SFC), structured text (ST) and instruction list (IL); its 2025 edition drops IL. Ladder is still common because, in Control Design's words, electricians "with little or no training" can follow each rung like a schematic. Source: [Control Design, A very short history of PLC programming platforms](https://www.controldesign.com/articles/2017/a-very-short-history-of-plc-programming-platforms/).

**The scan cycle.** A PLC does not react to inputs the instant they change. It loops. MITRE ATT&CK's page on the [I/O image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T0877/) describes it: during each scan "a PLC reads the status of all inputs and stores them in an image table", solves the whole logic program against that snapshot, then "updates the output image table" and writes it to the output modules. NIST puts control loop cycle times "in the order of milliseconds to minutes".

That snapshot matters for security: whoever controls the image tables controls what the logic believes and what the plant does. Stuxnet sat exactly there (lesson 9).

blocks.code:
Rung 1  Is the level below the low setpoint?
|----[ LT101 < LOW_SP ]----------------------------( LOW  )----|

Rung 2  Is the level at or above the high setpoint?
|----[ LT101 >= HIGH_SP ]--------------------------( HIGH )----|

Rung 3  Start on LOW, keep running (seal-in), stop on HIGH or E-stop
|----[ LOW ]------+----[/ HIGH ]----[/ ESTOP ]-----( PUMP )----|
|                 |
|----[ PUMP ]-----+

Legend:  [ X ]  normally open contact: passes power when X is true
         [/ X ] normally closed contact: passes power when X is false
         ( Y )  coil: Y becomes true if power reaches it
         LOW_SP = 200 cm, HIGH_SP = 300 cm (held in PLC registers)
blocks.caption: Ladder logic for the tank, written as text (real tools draw it graphically). Rung 3's parallel branch with the PUMP contact is a seal-in: once started, the pump keeps itself on until HIGH or the E-stop (emergency stop button) breaks the rung.

blocks.title: Six scans of the tank logic (setpoints 200 and 300 cm)
blocks.code:
# One PLC scan, repeated every few milliseconds
def scan(inputs, mem):
    # 1. read inputs into the input image
    LT101 = inputs["LT101"]
    ESTOP = inputs["ESTOP"]
    # 2. solve the logic, rung by rung
    LOW = LT101 < mem["LOW_SP"]               # rung 1
    HIGH = LT101 >= mem["HIGH_SP"]            # rung 2
    PUMP = (LOW or mem["PUMP"]) and not HIGH and not ESTOP  # rung 3
    # 3. write the output image to the output module
    mem["PUMP"] = PUMP
    return {"PUMP": PUMP}

scenes.caption: Scan at t=0: the input image holds level 210 and E-stop off. Inputs are copied once per scan, so the logic sees one consistent snapshot.
210 is neither below 200 nor at 300. The pump was off, so the seal-in branch is false too: PUMP stays off.
t=5: level 195 < 200, so LOW is true and rung 3 energises the pump.
t=10: level 220. LOW is false now, but PUMP from the last scan holds rung 3 on. This seal-in (latch) keeps the pump running between the setpoints.
t=30: level 320 >= 300, so HIGH opens the normally closed contact and the pump stops. At t=35 (305 cm) it stays off: no LOW, no seal-in.
Any scan with E-stop pressed forces PUMP false whatever the level (250 cm here). Values match the simulation in lesson 1 and were checked by running this function.

blocks.md: **Programs and modes.** The program lives in the PLC's memory and is created on the engineering workstation, then *downloaded* to the controller (and *uploaded* back to compare or back up). Many controllers have a physical **key switch**: NIST notes some PLCs "have physical key switches that are used to place the PLC in a mode that allows for programming changes", so a remote attacker cannot change logic while the key is in RUN. Lesson 11 shows what happened at a plant where the key was left in PROGRAM.

Changing a setpoint and changing the program are different. Setpoints are data the program reads (often over the network, by design, from the HMI). The program is the logic itself. Both can steer the process; defenders must watch and protect both.

blocks.prompt: In the ladder above, an attacker on the network cannot change the program but can write the HIGH_SP register. What can they make the tank do, and what still limits them?
blocks.reveal: They can raise HIGH_SP so the pump keeps running past 300 cm, overfilling the tank; or lower LOW_SP so it runs dry. The logic is unchanged and still obeys E-stop, and an **independent** safety system with its own sensor (lesson 8) can still trip. That is why safety functions must not depend on values the network can rewrite.

blocks.question: In the ladder, why does the pump keep running when the level is at 250 cm after starting at 195?
options: Because the PUMP contact in the parallel branch (seal-in) keeps rung 3 energised until HIGH or ESTOP breaks it
Because LOW is still true at 250
Because the HMI is holding the pump on
Because outputs are only written once a minute
blocks.explain: LOW is false at 250. The seal-in branch uses the pump's own state to stay on, which is how two-setpoint (hysteresis) control avoids switching the pump on and off rapidly around one value.

blocks.question: A PLC reads inputs into an image table at the start of each scan. If an attacker could change the input image after it is read but before the logic runs, what would the logic do?
options: Detect the change and fault
Act on the false values as if they were real measurements
Ignore the input image and read sensors directly
Stop scanning
blocks.explain: MITRE describes the image table as what the user program uses 'instead of directly interacting with physical I/O'. Manipulating it makes correct logic act on false inputs, the essence of Stuxnet's design.

lessons.title: The Purdue model: levels from field devices to the enterprise

blocks.md:
Plants have hundreds of devices. To decide who may talk to whom, defenders first sort them into layers. The most widely used sorting is the **Purdue model**. It comes from the *Purdue Reference Model for Computer Integrated Manufacturing* (1989), prepared by a committee of the International Purdue Workshop on Industrial Computer Systems (held at Purdue University in Indiana) and edited by Theodore J. Williams; hence the name. NIST notes the ISA-95 standard "grew from the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture (PERA), first published by ISA in 1992" (ISA is the International Society of Automation). The original is free at [pera.net](https://www.pera.net/Pera/PurdueReferenceModel/ReferenceModel.html).

The model was written to organise manufacturing computers, not for security. Security people later adopted its levels as natural network boundaries.

blocks.title: The Purdue model with DMZ, as drawn in NIST SP 800-82r3

nodes.label:
DMZ: historian replica,
patch server, jump host

scenes.caption: Start at the bottom: the physical process and Level 0, the sensors and actuators wired to it.
Level 1 holds the controllers that run the loops; beside them, the safety system with its own sensors and actuators.
Level 2 supervises an area: HMIs and SCADA servers. Level 3 runs the whole site: historian, engineering workstations, production scheduling.

Levels 4 and 5 are the business: ERP (enterprise resource planning), email, the internet. Between them and Level 3 sits a DMZ (demilitarized zone: a buffer network that neither side fully trusts) where data is handed over.

The rule NIST draws from the model: permit connections only between adjacent levels, and prevent Level 4 devices from talking directly to Levels 2, 1 or 0. A direct ERP-to-PLC path defeats the whole design.

blocks.md:
**The levels, bottom up** (as in NIST SP 800-82r3, Fig. 16):
- **Level 0, field I/O**: sensors and actuators.
- **Level 1, controller network**: PLCs, RTUs, safety controllers.
- **Level 2, area control**: HMIs and SCADA servers for one area of the plant.
- **Level 3, operations and control**: site-wide systems such as the historian and engineering workstations.
- **DMZ**: the boundary between operations and business. People often call it "Level 3.5"; NIST's figure simply labels it DMZ.
- **Level 4, business planning and logistics**, and **Level 5, enterprise**.

NIST's firewall guidance: rulesets "should be established to only permit connections between adjacent levels", and for a Purdue design, "prevent Level 4 devices from directly communicating with Level 2, 1, or 0 devices". It adds that outbound rules from the control network should be "as stringent as inbound rules".

blocks.code:
# Purdue levels from the top down; the DMZ sits between enterprise and operations.
ORDER = ["L5 enterprise", "L4 business", "DMZ", "L3 operations",
         "L2 area control", "L1 controllers", "L0 field I/O"]
ASSET = {"email server": "L5 enterprise", "ERP": "L4 business",
         "historian replica": "DMZ", "historian": "L3 operations",
         "eng workstation": "L3 operations", "HMI": "L2 area control",
         "PLC-1": "L1 controllers", "level sensor": "L0 field I/O"}

def check(src, dst):
    gap = abs(ORDER.index(ASSET[src]) - ORDER.index(ASSET[dst]))
    if gap <= 1:
        return "ok: same or adjacent level"
    return f"VIOLATION: skips {gap - 1} level(s)"

for src, dst in [("HMI", "PLC-1"), ("historian", "historian replica"),
                 ("ERP", "historian replica"), ("ERP", "PLC-1"),
                 ("eng workstation", "PLC-1")]:
    print(f"{src:16} to {dst:18} {check(src, dst)}")
blocks.caption: Runnable Python. Output: HMI to PLC-1, historian to replica and ERP to replica are adjacent; ERP to PLC-1 skips 3 levels; engineering workstation to PLC-1 skips 1 level.

blocks.prompt: The script flags 'eng workstation to PLC-1' as a violation. But engineers must program PLCs. Is the model wrong, or the plant?
blocks.reveal: Neither. The model is a guide, and real plants have legitimate flows that cross a level. The right response is to make such a flow an **explicit, documented, monitored exception**: only that workstation, only the vendor's programming protocol, ideally only during approved changes (and with the PLC key in PROGRAM only then). NIST's own SCADA example puts engineering workstations on the control center LAN next to the HMI. What must never exist is an *undocumented* path.

blocks.md: The Purdue model is a picture of function, not a security control. Drawing the levels changes nothing until firewalls, a DMZ and monitoring enforce them. Many breached plants had a Purdue diagram on the wall and a flat network in reality.

blocks.question: Under NIST's Purdue guidance, how should business users get production numbers from the plant historian?
options: Connect directly to the Level 3 historian from Level 4
Email the operators
Query the PLCs directly so the data is fresher
Read a replica of the historian in the DMZ, which the plant pushes data to
blocks.explain: Data is handed over in the DMZ so no business system connects into the control network. A replica historian (pushed from inside, ideally one way) is the classic pattern; lesson 13 adds unidirectional gateways.

blocks.question: Why does NIST say outbound rules from the control network should be as strict as inbound ones?
options: Because outbound traffic is always faster
Because PLCs send too many emails
Because an infected control-network machine that can reach the internet or enterprise freely gives attackers a channel out and a path back in
Because inbound rules do not work in OT
blocks.explain: Malware on a Level 2 or 3 host needs to talk to its operator. Strict egress filtering blocks that and limits what a compromised host can reach. NIST calls unmanaged outbound connections 'a significant risk'.

lessons.title: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment

blocks.md:
**ISA/IEC 62443** is the main international series of standards for securing industrial automation and control systems (IACS, the standard's own term for ICS). It was developed by the ISA99 committee together with IEC Technical Committee 65, Working Group 10, and covers the whole lifecycle for asset owners, product suppliers, integrators and service providers ([ISA overview](https://www.isa.org/standards-and-publications/isa-standards/isa-iec-62443-series-of-standards)).

Its central design idea is **zones and conduits**. In the words of Phoenix Contact's PLCnext documentation, which follows the standard: a **zone** is "a physical and/or logical group of system components to which the same security requirements apply", and a **conduit** is "a logical grouping of cyber assets dedicated exclusively to communications between two or more zones". Part 62443-3-2, *Security risk assessment for system design*, is where you draw them.

blocks.title: Zones joined only by conduits (ISA/IEC 62443 view)

scenes.caption: A zone groups assets with the same security requirements, physical or logical. Here: enterprise, DMZ, control center, basic process control (BPCS) and safety (SIS).
Zones talk only through conduits: defined, controlled communication channels (in practice firewalls, gateways, or a dedicated link) that carry their own security requirements.
Every zone and conduit gets a target security level (SL-T) from the risk assessment. The SIS zone, whose failure could kill people, gets the strictest target and the narrowest conduit.
Any path that does not go through a conduit is a design violation: here an office laptop reaching the PLC zone directly. The policy code below flags it.

blocks.md:
**How it differs from Purdue.** Purdue sorts by *function* (what level a device works at). Zones sort by *risk and requirements*: two PLCs at Level 1 can be in different zones if one runs a hazardous process. NIST SP 800-82r3 says organisations may segment by the Purdue model, ISA-95 levels, the three-tier IIoT (Industrial Internet of Things) architecture or "a combination", and applies its adjacent-only firewall rule to 62443 architectures too.

**Security levels.** Each zone and conduit is given a **target security level (SL-T)** from the risk assessment. After the controls are built, the **achieved level (SL-A)** is measured against it. The gap between SL-T and SL-A is the work list.

**Default deny.** The practical result is a table: for each pair of zones, the exact services allowed through the conduit, and nothing else.

blocks.caption: Runnable Python. Output: HMI to PLC over Modbus is allowed through the ops-to-control conduit; an office laptop to the PLC is denied and alerted; office to the DMZ replica over HTTPS is allowed; DMZ to an office file share is denied.

blocks.md: A conduit is a promise in two parts: only these services, between only these zones. Write it down as a table, enforce it with firewalls or gateways, and monitor it so that anything outside the table becomes an alert.

Zones are not VLANs. A VLAN (virtual LAN) is one way to separate traffic, but NIST lists VLANs as logical separation 'when physical separation may not be feasible'. A zone boundary needs an enforcement point, and a misconfigured switch trunk can quietly merge two zones.

blocks.question: Two PLCs both sit at Purdue Level 1. One runs packaging; the other controls a chlorine dosing pump. How might ISA/IEC 62443 treat them?
options: They may be put in different zones because their risks and security requirements differ, each with its own target security level
They must share a zone because they are at the same Purdue level
Neither needs a zone because PLCs are below the DMZ
Only the packaging PLC needs a zone
blocks.explain: Zones group assets with the same security requirements. A dosing controller with public-health consequences warrants a stricter zone and conduit than a packaging line, even at the same Purdue level.

blocks.question: In the policy code, a new vendor tool needs to read PLC values from the DMZ. What is the 62443-style way to allow it?
options: Add the vendor laptop to the control zone
Turn off the firewall during the visit
After a risk review, add one narrowly defined, monitored conduit entry, ideally serving the values from the historian rather than the PLC
Let the enterprise zone reach the PLC directly
blocks.explain: Every cross-zone flow is a conduit entry with a justification. The change is reviewed, scoped to the single service, and watched, rather than merging zones or disabling enforcement.

lessons.title: Modbus/TCP byte by byte, and why it trusts everyone

blocks.md:
**Modbus** is the simplest and most widespread industrial protocol. Modicon (now Schneider Electric) introduced it in 1979 and it remains a de facto standard: a request/reply protocol in which a client asks and a server (a PLC, drive or meter) answers. The Modbus Organization publishes the [application protocol specification](https://www.modbus.org/file/secure/modbusprotocolspecification.pdf) and the [TCP/IP implementation guide](https://www.modbus.org/file/secure/messagingimplementationguide.pdf); on Ethernet it runs on TCP port 502, which IANA registers under the name `mbap`.

**The data model** has four tables, each up to 65,536 entries addressed 0 to 65535:
- **Discrete inputs**: single bits, read-only (a limit switch).
- **Coils**: single bits, read-write (a pump run command).
- **Input registers**: 16-bit words, read-only (a level reading).
- **Holding registers**: 16-bit words, read-write (a setpoint).

How these map onto the PLC's own memory "is totally vendor device specific". For our tank: input register 0 is the level, holding registers 0 and 1 are HIGH_SP and LOW_SP.

**The frame.** A Modbus/TCP message is an ADU (application data unit) made of a 7-byte **MBAP header** (Modbus Application Protocol header) and a **PDU** (protocol data unit): one function code byte plus data.
- Transaction id (2 bytes), protocol id (2, always 0), length (2, counts the bytes that follow), unit id (1, for a device behind a gateway).
- **Function codes** include 01 Read Coils, 02 Read Discrete Inputs, 03 Read Holding Registers, 04 Read Input Registers, 05 Write Single Coil, 06 Write Single Register, 15 (0x0F) Write Multiple Coils, 16 (0x10) Write Multiple Registers, 22 (0x16) Mask Write Register, 23 (0x17) Read/Write Multiple Registers.
- An **exception** reply sets the top bit: function code + 0x80 (so 0x86 for a failed 06), followed by an exception code.

scenes.caption: Twelve bytes from a capture of the HMI talking to the tank PLC on TCP port 502. Every multi-byte field is big-endian: most significant byte first.
Transaction identifier 0x0002: the client picks it, the server copies it into the reply, so answers can be matched to questions.
Protocol identifier 0 means Modbus. Length 6 counts the bytes that follow: unit id plus PDU (1 + 5).
Unit identifier 1: which device behind a gateway should answer. These first 7 bytes are the MBAP header.
Function code 0x06, Write Single Register. This one byte is what a defender's rule keys on: is this a read or a write?
Register address 0 (the tank's HIGH_SP) and value 0x0140 = 320. Nothing in these 12 bytes says who sent them or proves they were allowed to.

blocks.code:
import struct

WRITE_CODES = {0x05: "Write Single Coil", 0x06: "Write Single Register",
               0x0F: "Write Multiple Coils", 0x10: "Write Multiple Registers",
               0x15: "Write File Record", 0x16: "Mask Write Register",
               0x17: "Read/Write Multiple Registers"}

def parse_modbus_tcp(frame: bytes) -> dict:
    if len(frame) < 8:
        raise ValueError("too short: MBAP header is 7 bytes plus a function code")
    tid, pid, length, unit = struct.unpack(">HHHB", frame[:7])  # big-endian
    if pid != 0:
        raise ValueError(f"protocol id {pid}: not Modbus")
    if length != len(frame) - 6:            # length counts unit id + PDU
        raise ValueError(f"length field {length} != {len(frame) - 6} bytes present")
    fc, data = frame[7], frame[8:]
    out = {"tid": tid, "unit": unit, "fc": fc, "data": data.hex(" ")}
    if fc & 0x80:                           # exception response
        out["exception"] = data[0]
    elif fc in (0x05, 0x06):                # address + value, 2 bytes each
        out["address"], out["value"] = struct.unpack(">HH", data[:4])
    out["write"] = (fc & 0x7F) in WRITE_CODES
    return out

frames = [  # bytes we built by hand, as a sniffer would capture them
    bytes.fromhex("0001 0000 0006 01 04 0000 0001"),  # read input register 0
    bytes.fromhex("0001 0000 0005 01 04 02 00fa"),    # reply: value 250
    bytes.fromhex("0002 0000 0006 01 06 0000 0140"),  # write holding reg 0 = 320
]
for f in frames:
    r = parse_modbus_tcp(f)
    print(r, "WRITE" if r["write"] else "")
blocks.caption: Runnable Python, checked. Output: the read request and its reply decode with write=False; the third frame decodes as fc 6, address 0, value 320, and is flagged WRITE. The bytes were built by hand to match the spec's field layout.

blocks.title: Modbus request and response, then a write from the wrong host

scenes.caption: The HMI (client) polls: function 04, read 1 input register at address 0. NIST would call this the normal, repetitive traffic of an OT network.
The PLC (server) answers with the same transaction id: 2 data bytes, 0x00FA = 250 cm.
An operator raises the high setpoint: function 06 writes holding register 0 = 320. The normal reply is an echo of the request.
A different host sends the same kind of write with value 380. Modbus has no field for identity or a password, so the PLC accepts and echoes it.

Defence: a passive monitor on a SPAN port (a switch port that mirrors traffic) or a network tap sees every packet without sending any. A write (FC 05, 06, 15, 16...) from a host that never writes is an alert.

blocks.md: **Why it trusts everyone.** Look at the fields again: none carries a user, a key, a signature or a sequence that a stranger could not guess. Any host that can open a TCP connection to port 502 can read and write. The TCP guide's only security feature is an optional "Access Control Module" that keeps "a list of authorized remote IP addresses", and IP addresses are easy to borrow on a flat network. CISA's alert on CrashOverride (lesson 10) states the consequence plainly: the malware "exploits the lack of authentication and authorization in common ICS protocols to issue unauthorized commands to field devices".

**Defender view.**
- *Prevent*: make sure only the HMI and engineering hosts can reach port 502 (lesson 5's conduit), and use protocol-aware firewalls that can allow reads but block writes from everyone else.
- *Detect*: alert on write function codes from unexpected sources, on unusual function codes (diagnostics, programming), and on new hosts talking Modbus (lesson 14 writes the Zeek and Suricata rules).
- *Respond*: compare current setpoints with the approved values in the historian or engineering records, and restore.

Encryption alone would not fix this. If any host can still connect and is trusted once connected, encrypting the write just hides the attack from your monitor. What is missing is authentication and authorisation of the sender, which Modbus/TCP Security adds (lesson 7).

blocks.question: Decode this request: `00 05 00 00 00 06 01 05 00 00 FF 00`. What does it ask for? (Function 05 uses 0xFF00 for ON and 0x0000 for OFF.)
options: Read coil 0
Write single coil 0 to ON
Write single register 0 to 65280
An exception reply
blocks.explain: Function code 0x05 is Write Single Coil; address 0x0000; value 0xFF00 means ON. In the tank this could be the pump's run coil, which is why a monitor should flag any write from a host that is not the HMI.

blocks.question: A server replies with function code 0x83 and one data byte 0x02. What happened?
options: A successful read of 2 registers
A new function code 0x83 the server supports
A write of value 2
An exception to a Read Holding Registers (03) request, with exception code 2
blocks.explain: Exception replies set the high bit: 0x80 + 0x03 = 0x83. Exception code 02 is 'illegal data address' in the spec. A burst of exceptions often means someone is probing addresses.

lessons.title: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design

blocks.md:
Modbus is not alone. NIST SP 800-82r3 sums up the field: "Many OT protocols have no authentication at any level. Without authentication, there is the potential to replay, modify, or spoof data or devices." Three more protocols you will meet:

**DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol 3)** runs between SCADA **masters** and **outstations** (RTUs and IEDs) in electric utilities, and also water, transport and oil and gas. The [DNP Users Group](https://www.dnp.org/About/Overview-of-DNP3-Protocol) says it was developed by Harris, Distributed Automation Products, handed to the users group in November 1993, and adopted as IEEE Std 1815 in 2010. IANA registers TCP port 20000 for it.

DNP3 later gained **Secure Authentication** (SAv5, based on IEC 62351-5, part of the IEC 62351 security series for power-system communication protocols). Its [specification](https://icscsi.org/library/Documents/ICS_Protocols/DNP3%20Secure%20Authentication%20v5%202011-11-08.pdf) lets an outstation "unambiguously determine it is communicating with a user who is authorized", using a challenge and a MAC (message authentication code, a keyed checksum), and is explicit: it "addresses authentication only, not encryption".

blocks.title: DNP3 Secure Authentication: challenge before a critical command

scenes.caption: The master sends a critical request, such as an operate command to a breaker. The outstation does not act on it yet.
The outstation issues a challenge containing random data that changes every time, which defeats replay.
The master replies with a MAC computed over the challenge and the request using a shared secret key. The outstation recomputes it, finds a match, and executes.
A rogue sender can copy the request but not the key. Its reply fails the check and the command is refused; the failure is a security event to log.

blocks.md: **S7comm (S7 Communication)** is "a Siemens proprietary protocol" between PLCs of the S7-300/400 family, used "for PLC programming, exchanging data between PLCs, accessing PLC data from SCADA" and diagnostics ([Wireshark wiki](https://wiki.wireshark.org/S7comm)). It rides on ISO-on-TCP (RFC 1006) at TCP port 102. Stuxnet (lesson 9) attacked the Windows library that Siemens' Step 7 software uses to speak to these PLCs.

**OPC UA (OPC Unified Architecture)** is the modern, secure-by-design option. OPC first stood for "OLE for Process Control" (OLE: Object Linking and Embedding, a Microsoft technology for sharing objects between programs; ESET's Industroyer report still uses that expansion for OPC DA, Data Access); NIST now expands OPC as Open Platform Communications. The [OPC UA security model](https://reference.opcfoundation.org/Core/Part2/v105/docs/4) gives each application an **ApplicationInstanceCertificate**, opens a **SecureChannel** whose keys then "encrypt and sign all Messages", authenticates users separately, and offers roles such as Operator, Engineer and SecurityAdmin. Security modes are "None", "Sign" and "SignAndEncrypt"; the spec says Profile None "shall be disabled by default". IANA registers TCP 4840 for it.

**Modbus/TCP Security** (port 802) puts Modbus inside TLS with X.509 certificates (the standard certificate format TLS uses) that carry a role, so the server can authorise each request.

blocks.title: What each protocol variant protects (1 = yes, 0 = no)

scenes.caption: Classic Modbus/TCP and plain DNP3: nothing. Any host that can reach the port can read, write, replay or spoof.
DNP3 Secure Authentication adds challenge and reply with a MAC: sender and message are verified, but by its own definition it does 'authentication only, not encryption'.
Modbus/TCP Security wraps Modbus in TLS with X.509 certificates and roles; OPC UA in SignAndEncrypt mode signs and encrypts every message. Both cover all three.
Simplified: the table shows what each design can do when enabled and configured. Old devices that cannot run it, or 'None' modes left on, fall back to the first row.

# Wireshark display filters a defender keeps at hand (field names from
# the Wireshark display filter reference). Use on captures from your own
# SPAN port or tap.

modbus.exception_code                          # any exception reply (probing?)
mbtcp && tcp.dstport == 502 && ip.src != 10.2.0.10   # requests not from the HMI
s7comm.param.func == 0xf0                       # S7comm 'setup communication'

dnp3 && !(ip.addr == 10.2.0.11)                 # DNP3 not involving the master
