blocks.caption: Display filters, not capture filters. The addresses are the toy plant's HMI (10.2.0.10), master (10.2.0.11) and engineering workstation (10.2.0.30). Exception replies are the ones where the server added 0x80 to the function code.

blocks.md: Secure protocols only help when they are on. An OPC UA server left in mode None, a DNP3 outstation without SAv5 keys, or a Modbus/TCP Security device that also listens on plain port 502 gives the attacker the old, unauthenticated path.

Ask two questions of any industrial protocol: does the receiver verify who sent this command, and can it tell if the command was changed or replayed? For classic Modbus and plain DNP3 the answer is no, so the network around them must do that job.

blocks.question: A utility enables DNP3 Secure Authentication. An attacker can still sniff the link. What can they still do?
options: Read the measurements and commands in clear text, but not forge or replay critical commands without the key
Nothing: SAv5 encrypts all traffic
Forge operate commands because SAv5 only checks the master's IP
Change the MAC algorithm
blocks.explain: SAv5 authenticates critical messages with a challenge and MAC, defeating spoofing, modification and replay, but its spec says it addresses authentication only, not encryption. Confidentiality needs TLS or link encryptors.

blocks.question: An OPC UA server supports SignAndEncrypt but also exposes an endpoint in mode None. What is the risk?
options: None: clients always pick the strongest mode
A client or attacker can connect without signatures or encryption, bypassing the protections
Mode None encrypts but does not sign
It only affects performance
blocks.explain: Security modes are chosen per connection. Leaving None enabled leaves an unprotected door; the specification says the None profile is for testing and should be disabled by default when secure profiles are available.

lessons.title: How attacks on physical processes work

blocks.md:
An attack on a plant is only "industrial" when it changes the physical process. This lesson stays at concept level: what the attacker changes and what the defender sees. MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, the public knowledge base of adversary behaviour in industrial systems that lesson 16 tours, names the building blocks:
- **Modify Parameter**: "Adversaries may modify parameters used to instruct industrial control system devices", such as setpoints, limits and timers.
- **Manipulation of View**: "Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the information reported back to operators or controllers", so humans keep trusting a false picture.
- **Manipulation of Control**: "Adversaries may manipulate physical process control within the industrial environment."
- **Loss of Safety**: compromising the safety functions "designed to maintain safe operation of a process when unacceptable or dangerous conditions occur".

**The core trick is combining them.** Changing a setpoint alone is noisy: operators see the level climb and intervene. Changing it *while the HMI shows normal values* removes the human from the loop. Ralph Langner, an industrial control security researcher who analysed Stuxnet, describes exactly this in [To Kill a Centrifuge](https://web.archive.org/web/20201223151646/https://www.langner.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/to-kill-a-centrifuge.pdf): sensor values were "recorded for a period of 21 seconds", then "replayed in a constant loop", showing on SCADA screens and "suggesting normal operation to human operators and any software-implemented alarm routines".

The toy scenario below applies the same idea to our tank. The numbers are illustrative, computed from the 5 cm per minute net fill rate of lesson 1.

blocks.title: Concept: a setpoint change hidden behind a replayed HMI view

scenes.caption: Normal operation: the level cycles between the setpoints, the HMI shows live values, the safety system watches its own level sensor (trip at 360 cm, a high-high level above the normal high setpoint).
Minute 10: an unauthorised write sets HIGH_SP to 380 (ATT&CK: Modify Parameter). At the same moment the HMI starts showing replayed, normal-looking values (Manipulation of View).
Minute 20: the pump never stops, so the real level climbs 5 cm per minute to 330 cm, while the operator sees about 270. The operator is calm because the screen is lying.
Minute 26: the independent safety system's own sensor reads 360 cm and trips, stopping the pump. Its logic and sensor were never on the path the attacker controlled, so it still works.

blocks.md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

**Defender view.**
- *Prevent*: only the HMI may write setpoints (conduits, protocol-aware firewall); engineering limits in the PLC logic refuse out-of-range setpoints (a high setpoint above the tank's safe height should be rejected by the program itself).
- *Detect*: alert on writes from unexpected hosts; compare the HMI with an **independent** measurement (the SIS's own transmitter read one way, a local gauge, the historian fed by a separate path); check physics: a running pump must raise the level.
- *Respond*: treat the HMI as untrusted, check the process with local instruments and walk-downs, move to manual control if needed (lesson 15).

blocks.code:
# Compare what the HMI shows with a second, independent level sensor
# (for example the safety system's own transmitter, read over a one-way link).
TOLERANCE = 15     # cm: normal disagreement between two healthy sensors
FILL_RATE = 5      # cm/min the level must rise when the pump runs

samples = [  # minute, HMI level, independent level, pump running?
    (8, 268, 270, True), (10, 271, 280, True), (12, 270, 290, True),
    (14, 268, 300, True), (16, 271, 310, True), (18, 270, 320, True),
]
prev = None
for t, hmi, indep, pump in samples:
    alerts = []
    if abs(hmi - indep) > TOLERANCE:
        alerts.append(f"sensors disagree by {abs(hmi - indep)} cm")
    if prev and pump:
        dt = t - prev[0]
        if hmi - prev[1] < FILL_RATE * dt / 2:  # far too flat for a running pump
            alerts.append("HMI level not rising while pump runs")
    print(t, hmi, indep, "; ".join(alerts) or "ok")
    prev = (t, hmi)
blocks.caption: Runnable Python, checked. Output: minute 8 ok; from minute 10 the HMI value stays flat while the pump runs, and from minute 12 the two sensors disagree by 20, 32, 39, then 50 cm. Either signal alone justifies a call to the control room.

blocks.question: Why did the replay in the scenario defeat the operator but not the safety system?
options: The safety system ignores sensors
Safety systems cannot be attacked
The replay was too slow
The SIS used its own sensor and logic, which were not on the path the attacker manipulated
blocks.explain: The replay changed what the HMI displayed. The SIS read the real level through its own transmitter and acted independently. Triton (lesson 11) shows attackers going after that last layer too, which is why its independence matters so much.

blocks.question: Which single check would have caught the attack earliest in the scenario?
options: Waiting for the HMI high-level alarm
A monthly review of historian trends
A monitoring rule on Modbus writes from hosts other than the HMI
Rebooting the HMI
blocks.explain: The write happened at minute 10 and produced a network event at once. The HMI alarm would never fire because the HMI showed replayed data, and monthly reviews are far too slow.

lessons.title: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied

blocks.md:
**Stuxnet** is the case that made ICS security a field. Symantec's analysts Nicolas Falliere, Liam O Murchu and Eric Chien reverse-engineered it in the [W32.Stuxnet Dossier](https://docs.broadcom.com/doc/security-response-w32-stuxnet-dossier-11-en) (version 1.4, February 2011). Its "final goal is to reprogram industrial control systems (ICS) by modifying code on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to make them work in a manner the attacker intended and to hide those changes from the operator".

**What was found.** Stuxnet was discovered in July 2010 and existed at least a year earlier; the earliest sample is from June 2009. Symantec's monitoring found about 60% of infected hosts in Iran. Ralph Langner's analysis, *To Kill a Centrifuge* (2013), ties the payloads to the uranium enrichment plant at Natanz, Iran.

**How it reached the controllers.** The key targets were *Field PGs*, which the dossier describes as Windows computers "used to program PLCs" and usually not networked. Stuxnet spread over the LAN and, for the last hop, by USB drive, using a Windows shortcut (LNK) flaw, CVE-2010-2568 (patched in Microsoft security bulletin MS10-046), and the Print Spooler flaw CVE-2010-2729 (MS10-061), among four then-unpatched Windows vulnerabilities. Its drivers were signed with certificates stolen from Realtek and JMicron so Windows would trust them.

**What it did to the plant** (Symantec, sequence A). On a Siemens S7-315-2 PLC with CP 342-5 communication modules for Profibus (a standard industrial network bus) driving banks of frequency converters (variable-speed motor drives from Vacon or Fararo Paya), Stuxnet injected its own code blocks into the PLC program, including the main cyclic block OB1, so its code ran at the start of every scan. It recorded normal operation, then rewrote drive parameters "remotely configured via Profibus" to swing the motor speed.

**How it hid.** The PLC rootkit lived in a fake copy of `s7otbxdx.dll`, the Windows library Step 7 uses to talk to PLCs. It intercepted requests to read program blocks and skipped its own, so "victims attempting to verify the issue would not see any rogue PLC code". Langner describes a second, earlier attack on S7-417 controllers of the centrifuge protection system that recorded 21 seconds of sensor values and replayed them to the screens during the attack (lesson 8).

blocks.title: Stuxnet's drive-speed sequence on an S7-315 (Symantec dossier)

scenes.caption: First the infected PLC only watches. It counts records from the frequency converters and waits until about 13 days of operation between 807 and 1210 Hz have been seen.
Sequence 1 sets the drives' maximum frequency to 1410 Hz, above the normal range, then normal operation resumes. Short sequences are drawn wider than real time so they are visible.
About 27 days later, sequence 2 sets 2 Hz, then 1064 Hz: the motors are slowed almost to a stop and sped up again. The dossier: Stuxnet sabotages 'by slowing down or speeding up the motor'.
Then the cycle repeats, about every 27 days. All the while, an engineer reading the PLC through the infected Step 7 software sees the original program: the rootkit hides the added blocks.

blocks.md: Stuxnet attacked at the two places defenders trusted most: the engineering software (so the program looked unchanged) and the operator's view (so the process looked normal). The defence is verification through a path the attacker does not control.

**Defender view.**
- *Prevent*: control removable media into the plant (scanning stations, allowlisting on engineering hosts); keep engineering workstations patched and isolated; lock PLC programming with key switches or passwords.
- *Detect*: compare PLC logic with an approved offline backup, read with a **clean** machine, not the plant's possibly infected workstation; watch for program downloads and new blocks outside change windows; cross-check process values against independent instruments.
- *Respond*: restore known-good logic from offline backups; rebuild engineering hosts.

MITRE ATT&CK for ICS lists Stuxnet under Replication Through Removable Media, Rootkit, Modify Program, Program Download, Modify Parameter and Manipulation of View.

blocks.caption: Runnable Python. Output: 'FC9: NEW block, not in approved backup' and 'OB1: CHANGED since approved backup'. Block names and contents are invented; real tools export project blocks for hashing in vendor-specific ways.

blocks.question: An engineer uploads the PLC program through the plant's engineering workstation and it matches the approved version exactly. Why might that not be enough after a Stuxnet-style infection?
options: The workstation's PLC communication library may be intercepted, so the tool shows a cleaned view while the PLC runs extra code
Uploads are always encrypted
PLCs cannot store more than one program
Hashes cannot be computed for PLC code
blocks.explain: Stuxnet's fake s7otbxdx.dll hid its blocks from Step 7 reads. Verification must use a trusted path: a clean machine, vendor integrity features, or physical inspection of behaviour.

blocks.question: Why did Stuxnet need removable media at all?
options: USB is faster than Ethernet
Siemens PLCs only accept code from USB
The machines that program the PLCs were typically not connected to untrusted networks, so a USB drive could carry it the last hop
To avoid antivirus
blocks.explain: Symantec: propagation through removable drives covered 'the last and final hop to a Field PG that is never connected to an untrusted network'. An air gap without media controls is a speed bump, not a wall.

blocks.md:
**Ukraine, 23 December 2015.** A US team from ICS-CERT (the Industrial Control Systems Cyber Emergency Response Team), US-CERT (the US Computer Emergency Readiness Team), the Department of Energy, the FBI and NERC (the North American Electric Reliability Corporation) interviewed staff at six Ukrainian organisations. Their [public alert](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-alerts/ir-alert-h-16-056-01) reports outages "caused by remote cyber intrusions at three regional electric power distribution companies (Oblenergos) impacting approximately 225,000 customers". NIST calls it "the first known cyber attack on a power grid".

Notice what the attackers did *not* need to open the breakers: no ICS malware, no protocol tricks, just the operators' own tools over their own VPN with stolen credentials. (Custom firmware came only to disable converters.) The analysis by the SANS Institute (a security training organisation) and the E-ISAC (Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center) adds that the utilities restored service in hours by moving to manual operations.

blocks.title: Ukraine, 23 December 2015: from phishing to dark substations

scenes.caption: Before the attack: spear-phishing emails with malicious Microsoft Office attachments delivered BlackEnergy 3 malware (a remote-access trojan family) to the companies' IT networks. Its exact role is unknown; investigators suspect credential theft.
With legitimate credentials acquired beforehand, the attackers entered the control networks through VPN connections.
Within 30 minutes at three distribution companies, people operated breakers remotely through existing admin tools or the ICS client software itself. About 225,000 customers lost power.

To slow recovery: KillDisk wiped systems including Windows HMIs embedded in RTUs, serial-to-Ethernet converters got corrupted firmware, and server UPS (uninterruptible power supply) units were scheduled to switch off.
A telephone flood kept customers from reporting outages. Operators restored power in hours by going to substations and running them manually.

blocks.md:
**Industroyer, 17 December 2016.** A year later a substation near Kyiv lost power for about an hour (NIST). Anton Cherepanov of ESET, a security company, analysed the malware, named it **Industroyer** ([report](https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf)); the ICS security firm Dragos named it **CrashOverride**. Unlike 2015, it spoke standard telecontrol and substation protocols itself: modules for IEC 60870-5-101, IEC 60870-5-104, IEC 61850 and OPC DA, so it could "directly control switches and circuit breakers". It also carried a data wiper, a denial-of-service tool against Siemens SIPROTEC protective relays, and an activation timestamp of 17 December 2016. ESET notes its backdoor could be set to talk to its controllers only at chosen hours, for example outside working hours.

CISA's [CrashOverride alert](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2017/06/12/crashoverride-malware): "This malware exploits the lack of authentication and authorization in common ICS protocols to issue unauthorized commands to field devices."

It is tempting to read 2015 as 'malware turned off the lights'. Investigators found BlackEnergy but could not show it played a role in the outage; people turned off the lights, through legitimate remote access. Monitoring that only looks for malware would have missed it.

**Defender view.** From the CISA alert and the SANS analysis:
- *Prevent*: limit remote access; CISA: remote access "should be operator controlled, time limited", no persistent vendor connections, strong multi-factor authentication; isolate ICS networks from untrusted networks, using a data diode where one-way flow suffices; application allowlisting on HMIs.
- *Detect*: VPN logins to OT outside approved work, operator accounts used remotely, breaker commands from unusual consoles; for Industroyer-style tools, IEC 104 or 61850 commands from hosts that never send them.
- *Respond*: plans that "include the assumption that the ICS is actively working counter to the safe operation of the process", and practised manual operation.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime

# Approved remote sessions into the control network, from the change system.
APPROVED = {("vendor-ana", "2025-12-23")}           # (user, day)
OT_HOSTS = {"10.2.0.10", "10.2.0.11"}               # HMI and SCADA server

sessions = [  # from the VPN concentrator and the HMI's own login log
    {"user": "vendor-ana", "start": "2025-12-23 10:02", "target": "10.2.0.11"},
    {"user": "dispatch-3", "start": "2025-12-23 15:31", "target": "10.2.0.10"},
    {"user": "dispatch-3", "start": "2025-12-23 15:33", "target": "10.2.0.11"},
]

for s in sessions:
    t = datetime.strptime(s["start"], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
    reasons = []
    if s["target"] in OT_HOSTS and (s["user"], t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")) not in APPROVED:
        reasons.append("remote session to OT with no approved change")
    if s["user"].startswith("dispatch"):
        reasons.append("operator account used over VPN (operators work on site)")
    print(s["start"], s["user"], "->", s["target"], "|", "; ".join(reasons) or "ok")
blocks.caption: Runnable Python (toy data, invented names and a 2025 date). Output: the vendor's approved session is ok; both dispatcher sessions are flagged: no approved change, and an operator account in use over VPN.

blocks.question: In the 2015 attack, which control would most directly have blocked the breaker operations?
options: Antivirus signatures for BlackEnergy on substation RTUs
Requiring multi-factor authentication and operator-controlled, time-limited approval for any remote access into the control network
Encrypting the historian
Faster patching of office PCs
blocks.explain: The breakers were opened by humans using stolen credentials over VPN and legitimate tools. Strong MFA plus approval-gated, time-limited remote access attacks that path directly; the investigators could not tie the outage to BlackEnergy's capabilities.

blocks.question: Why did ESET judge Industroyer more dangerous than the 2015 toolset?
options: It encrypted files for ransom
It was signed with stolen certificates
It spread by USB
It implemented four industrial protocols itself, so it could command switches and breakers directly without the operators' software
blocks.explain: ESET: the authors 'went to great lengths to create malware capable of directly controlling switches and circuit breakers', speaking IEC 101, IEC 104, IEC 61850 and OPC DA. A tool like that can be reused at other utilities with the same protocols.

lessons.title: Case: Triton and the attack on a safety system

blocks.md:
Lesson 8 ended with the safety system as the last line of defence. In 2017 someone went after that line. Mandiant, an incident response company then part of FireEye, responded to the incident and published [the first analysis](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/attackers-deploy-new-ics-attack-framework-triton/) in December 2017: an attack framework "built to interact with Triconex Safety Instrumented System (SIS) controllers", made by Schneider Electric. The malware is known as **Triton** (named for the Triconex controllers it targeted, per MIT Technology Review), **Trisis**, and **HatMan** (CISA's name).

Mandiant explains why this matters: "If the SIS and DCS controls fail, the final line of defense is the design of the industrial facility", meaning rupture discs, physical alarms and emergency procedures. An attacker who can disable the SIS and then push the process into a hazard through the DCS could cause "the maximum amount of damage allowed by the physical and mechanical safeguards".

blocks.title: Triton: why an integrated SIS and a PROGRAM key mattered

scenes.caption: Mandiant: the attacker first held a foothold on the plant's process control (DCS) network, which could have been used to shut the plant down, but went further.

They gained remote access to the SIS engineering workstation, a Windows machine that could reach the safety controllers over the network, and ran Triton disguised as Trilog, a legitimate log-viewing tool.
Triton spoke the proprietary TriStation protocol to add a program to the controllers' memory. It worked because the controllers would accept program changes: the physical key was in PROGRAM.

Redundant processors found mismatched code, failed a validation check and did their job: a safe shutdown. The first trip, in June 2017, was blamed on a mechanical fault; only after a second in August did the owners call in investigators.
Mandiant's fixes: keys in RUN except during approved work, no network path from DCS to the SIS workstation, and a one-way gateway for anything that needs SIS data.

blocks.md: **Where and who.** MIT Technology Review places the plant in Saudi Arabia, with a first shutdown in June 2017 and a second in August. CISA's [advisory AA22-083A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-083a) says actors tied to TsNIIKhM (Central Scientific Research Institute of Chemistry and Mechanics), a Russian government research institute, used Triton on "a foreign oil refinery's" safety controllers, which "resulted in the refinery shutting down for several days". An indictment unsealed by the US Department of Justice on 24 March 2022 charges Evgeny Gladkikh, a programmer at TsNIIKhM. The indictment does not name the victim, calling it "victim company 1"; [CSO Online reports](https://www.csoonline.com/article/3654833/u-s-charges-russian-government-agents-for-cyber-attacks-on-critical-infrastructure.html) that researchers believe it was Saudi Arabia's Petro Rabigh. Prosecutors allege the aim was physical damage, with the shutdowns an unintended giveaway.

**How it failed.** Mandiant: the SIS controllers "initiated a safe shutdown when application code between redundant processing units failed a validation check". NIST describes this as triple-redundant processors spotting mismatched code. MIT Technology Review adds that workers had left the physical keys in a position that allowed remote programming.

The safety system worked as designed: it detected an inconsistency and failed safe. The lesson is not that safety systems are weak, but that their independence from the networks attackers can reach is the property to protect above all.

**Defender view** (Mandiant's recommendations):
- Where feasible, segregate safety system networks from process control and IT; SIS engineering workstations "should not be dual-homed" (connected to two networks at once).
- Use the physical key: "keys should not be left in the PROGRAM mode other than during scheduled programming events"; put key changes under change management and "audit current key state regularly".
- Use a unidirectional gateway for any application that needs SIS data.
- Apply strict access control and application allowlisting on every endpoint that can reach the SIS over TCP/IP.
- Detection: TriStation traffic from any host other than the approved workstation, controller mode changes, and unexplained SIS trips, which deserve a security look as well as a process one.

blocks.caption: Runnable Python. Output: SIS-1 in PROGRAM during its approved window is ok; SIS-1 still in PROGRAM the next morning raises an alert; SIS-2 in RUN is ok.

blocks.question: Mandiant notes the attacker already had a foothold on the DCS and could have shut the plant down from there. Why go after the SIS instead?
options: Compromising both control and safety could let them create a hazard while preventing the safety system from stopping it, causing physical damage
The SIS stores billing data
The SIS was easier to reach
To install ransomware
blocks.explain: Mandiant judged the long-term goal was a physical consequence. Shutting a plant down costs money; disabling the SIS while the DCS drives the process into an unsafe state could destroy equipment or harm people.

blocks.question: Which single change would have most directly prevented the program change on the Triconex controllers?
options: Faster internet at the plant
Keeping the controllers' key switch in RUN except during approved programming
A bigger historian
Disabling the HMI screensaver
blocks.explain: With the key in RUN the controller refuses program changes from the network, whatever the attacker controls upstream. Mandiant made this its second recommendation.

lessons.title: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon

blocks.md:
NIST describes how OT moved from isolated, proprietary systems to "industry standard computers, OSs, and network protocols" with "corporate connectivity and remote access capabilities". This **IT/OT convergence** brings data and convenience, and also brings IT's attackers. Four cases show four ways it goes wrong.

**1. Colonial Pipeline, May 2021: IT ransomware, OT shutdown.** Colonial carries refined fuel through about 5,500 miles of pipeline, nearly half the fuel used on the US East Coast, per CEO Joseph Blount's [Senate testimony](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/imo/media/doc/Testimony-Blount-2021-06-08.pdf). The DarkSide ransomware gang encrypted IT systems; NIST says entry was through "a legacy VPN profile". The company stopped the pipeline itself to protect the OT network.

blocks.title: Colonial Pipeline, May 2021: an IT incident that stopped the OT

scenes.caption: Friday 7 May, just before 5:00 AM EDT: an employee finds a ransom note on a system in the IT network and tells the control center's operations supervisor. Short events are drawn wider than real time.
From about 5:55 AM staff begin shutting down; by 6:10 AM all 5,500 miles of pipeline are stopped, to stop the malware reaching the OT network 'if it had not already'.
The company pays the DarkSide ransom to have every recovery tool available, while scanning systems and patrolling the pipeline by air and road because 'our OT was not visible'.
Wednesday evening, 12 May: restart begins. CISA and FBI had said there was no indication the OT was directly affected; the outage came from losing trust in IT systems it depended on.

blocks.md: **2. Oldsmar, Florida, February 2021: a remote-access screen, and a later doubt.** CISA's [advisory AA21-042A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa21-042a) reported that on 5 February "unidentified cyber actors obtained unauthorized access" to a water treatment plant's SCADA system and used it "to increase the amount of sodium hydroxide", a caustic chemical. Staff "immediately noticed the change in dosing amounts and corrected the issue". The advisory pointed to desktop sharing software (possibly TeamViewer), weak passwords and Windows 7.

In 2023, Al Braithwaite, the city manager at the time, called it a "nonevent" that may have been an employee's mistake, and the FBI said it "was not able to confirm that this incident was initiated by a targeted cyber intrusion" ([WUSF report](https://www.wusf.org/local-state/2023-04-13/official-hack-oldsmar-city-water-treatment-plant-2021)). The county sheriff's office said the case was still open. Treat Oldsmar as a lesson in exposure (remote desktop on a SCADA PC, shared weak passwords) and in caution: early claims of attack can be wrong.

**3. Unitronics PLCs, November 2023: the PLC on the internet.** CISA's [advisory AA23-335A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-335a): actors using the persona CyberAv3ngers, affiliated with Iran's IRGC (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps), compromised Israeli-made Unitronics Vision PLCs with built-in HMIs, including at US water facilities. The devices were "internet-facing, used Unitronics' default passwords or no password", on the default TCP port 20256. The attackers put a defacement image on the HMI screen, which hid the readings operators needed.

**4. Volt Typhoon, 2024: waiting inside.** [Microsoft names threat actors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-threat-actor-naming) after weather, and "Typhoon indicates origin or attribution to China". CISA, the NSA (National Security Agency) and the FBI's [advisory AA24-038A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-038a) assessed "with high confidence" that this actor was "pre-positioning themselves on IT networks to enable lateral movement to OT assets to disrupt functions", in communications, energy, transportation and water, holding some footholds "for at least five years". They lived off the land (used built-in admin tools instead of malware) and tested "default OT vendor credentials".

blocks.caption: Runnable Python: audit only addresses you own. Ports from IANA (502 mbap, 802 mbap-s, 102 iso-tsap, 20000 dnp, 4840 opcua-tcp) and AA23-335A (20256). Output: the website is clean; the OPC UA endpoint and the Unitronics device are flagged with CISA's fixes.

blocks.md: CISA's 2025 primary mitigations for OT read like a summary of these four cases: remove OT connections to the public internet, change default passwords, secure remote access, segment IT and OT, and practise operating manually.

blocks.question: Colonial's OT was not shown to be infected, yet the pipeline stopped for five days. What design lesson does CISA's advisory AA21-131A draw?
options: OT should share IT's ransomware backups
Move OT to the cloud
Pay ransoms faster
Ensure the OT network can operate at necessary capacity even if the IT network is compromised, with robust IT/OT segmentation and tested manual controls
blocks.explain: CISA and FBI urged that OT be able to keep running when IT is compromised, plus segmentation, a DMZ and regularly tested manual controls. Dependence on IT systems, not OT damage, drove the outage.

blocks.question: What made the Unitronics compromises possible, according to CISA?
options: A zero-day in Modbus
Stolen certificates
Internet-facing PLCs with default or no passwords on default ports
Insider sabotage
blocks.explain: No advanced exploit was needed. Removing the devices from the internet and changing default passwords would have stopped this campaign; CISA's primary mitigations list exactly these.

lessons.title: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting

blocks.md:
Every case so far ended with the attacker reaching a controller over a network that should not have allowed it. The first family of defences shapes that network. CISA's 2025 [primary mitigations for OT](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/primary-mitigations-reduce-cyber-threats-operational-technology) put it simply: "Segment IT and OT networks", introducing "a demilitarized zone for passing control data to enterprise logistics".

**Segmentation and DMZ.** NIST SP 800-82r3: use firewalls (and unidirectional gateways) between levels or zones, permit only connections between adjacent ones, and make outbound rules as strict as inbound. The DMZ is where IT and OT meet without either connecting into the other: replica historian, patch server, and a jump host (a hardened server that remote users log in to first, the only one allowed to open sessions further in).

**Unidirectional gateways (data diodes).** NIST's glossary: "The hardware permits data to flow from one network to another but is physically unable to send any information at all back to the source network." Unlike a firewall, it "cannot be programmed to allow data to flow in both directions because the hardware is incapable". Software on each side replicates databases or emulates servers so that applications still work.

scenes.caption: Before: office PCs, the VPN, the HMI, the PLC and even the safety system share one flat network. It works, and it is how many plants grew.

The problem: any foothold anywhere reaches everything. A phished office PC or a stolen VPN password can reach the HMIs and talk Modbus straight to the PLC: the kind of path the Ukraine attackers used and Volt Typhoon prepared.
After: an IT/OT firewall and a DMZ separate the business from the plant. Office users read a replica historian in the DMZ; nothing in IT connects into OT.
Data leaves through a unidirectional gateway: hardware that can send out but is physically unable to send anything back, so nothing can ride the data path inward.
Remote support lands on a jump host in the DMZ after MFA, and reaches the engineering workstation only when an approved, time-limited session is opened.
Inside, a protocol-aware firewall lets only the HMI and the engineering workstation reach the PLC. The SIS has no routed path at all.

blocks.code:
# OT boundary policy for the toy plant (first match wins, default deny)
#  #  from              to                service                  action  log
   1  HIST-1            DMZ replica       via one-way gateway      (hardware: no return path)
   2  Enterprise        DMZ replica       HTTPS 443                allow   yes
   3  Vendor (VPN+MFA)  DMZ jump host     RDP 3389                 allow   yes
   4  DMZ jump host     EWS-1             RDP 3389                 allow   yes  # only while a change ticket is open
   5  HMI-1             PLC-1             Modbus 502, reads        allow   no
   6  HMI-1             PLC-1             Modbus 502, writes       allow   yes
   7  EWS-1             PLC-1             vendor programming       allow   yes  # key switch to PROGRAM only for the change
   8  any               PLC-1             Modbus 502, writes       deny    alert
   9  any OT zone       internet          any                      deny    alert
  10  any               SIS zone          any                      deny    alert
  11  any               any               any                      deny    yes
blocks.caption: A zone policy table for the 'after' design, written as a reviewable document rather than vendor syntax. RDP is Microsoft's Remote Desktop Protocol. Rules 5 to 8 need a protocol-aware (deep packet inspection) firewall that can tell a Modbus read from a write.

blocks.md:
**Application allowlisting.** Only approved programs may run. NIST notes "the relatively static nature of OT environments" makes allowlisting practical, and the Ukraine alert calls HMI and database servers "ideal candidates". Ransomware and droppers fail to start even if they arrive.

**Secure remote access.** CISA: if remote access is essential, use a private connection with a VPN, a strong password and phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA). The Ukraine alert adds: remote access "should be operator controlled, time limited, and procedurally similar to 'lock out, tag out'", the physical-safety practice of locking and labelling equipment before work, and "remote persistent vendor connections should not be allowed into the control network".

**Safety system independence.** Mandiant after Triton: segregate safety networks, no dual-homed SIS workstations, one-way gateways for SIS data, keys in RUN.

A firewall rule that says 'allow 10.0.0.0/8 to OT, any port, temporary' is the most common way segmentation fails. Review the rule table regularly, expire temporary rules automatically, and alert on hits to rule 11: traffic nobody planned is either a misconfiguration or an intruder.

Segment so that the office cannot reach the controllers, pass data out through a DMZ (one way where possible), let in remote support only through an approved, timed, MFA-protected door, and keep the safety system off every routed path.

blocks.question: A plant wants dashboards in the head office showing live tank levels, and wants no possible inbound path. Which design fits?
options: A unidirectional gateway pushing historian data to a replica in the DMZ, read by the head office
A firewall rule allowing the head office to query the PLCs
A VPN from head office into the control zone
Putting the PLCs on the internet behind a password
blocks.explain: A data diode is physically one-way, so the replica can be fed without any route back into OT. Firewalls and VPNs can be misconfigured to allow inbound traffic; a diode cannot.

blocks.question: In the policy table, why is rule 8 (deny writes from any host) placed after rules 5 to 7?
options: Rule order does not matter
So that writes are logged twice
First match wins: the specific allows for the HMI and engineering workstation must come before the general deny, or they would be blocked too
Because deny rules must always be last-but-one
blocks.explain: With first-match evaluation, a broad deny placed earlier would shadow the narrow allows. The usual pattern is specific allows, then specific denies with alerts, then a final default deny.

lessons.title: Watching OT: asset inventory and passive monitoring

blocks.md: You cannot defend devices you do not know about. CISA's August 2025 [asset inventory guidance](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/foundations-ot-cybersecurity-asset-inventory-guidance-owners-and-operators) defines an **asset inventory** as "an organized, regularly updated list of an organization's systems, hardware, and software", supplemented by an **OT taxonomy** that classifies assets "based on function and criticality". NIST adds the attributes that matter for vulnerabilities: vendor, model, firmware, operating system and software versions (lesson 2 showed a toy inventory).

**How to build it without breaking things.** NIST SP 800-82r3 contrasts two methods:
- **Passive scanning** "inspects existing network traffic" from switch mirror ports or taps and "does not introduce any additional traffic", which is ideal because OT devices "may exhibit unexpected behavior when directly probed". It can reveal manufacturers, part numbers and firmware, but misses silent devices and can take days.
- **Active scanning** probes devices; NIST urges "extreme caution" because scans "may cause device instability", and suggests scheduling them in planned outages.

**Monitoring.** OT traffic is "more deterministic (i.e., repeatable, predictable, and designed) than IT network traffic", so NIST suggests learning the normal state first, in a passive "listen or learning" mode, then alerting on what is new. Sensors usually sit on SPAN (switched port analyzer) ports or passive taps at zone boundaries. Host monitoring on HMIs, SCADA servers and engineering workstations helps where it does not harm performance. NIST also warns that automatic blocking by an IPS (intrusion prevention system) can itself disrupt OT, and suggests considering placing it higher up, for example at the DMZ interfaces.

Two open-source tools understand Modbus out of the box:
- **Zeek**, a network analysis framework that turns traffic into logs. Its Modbus analyzer writes a `modbus.log` with the transaction id, unit, function name (for example `WRITE_SINGLE_REGISTER`), request or response, and exceptions ([docs](https://docs.zeek.org/en/master/scripts/base/protocols/modbus/main.zeek.html)).
- **Suricata**, an intrusion detection engine whose rules can match `modbus: access write` and more ([docs](https://docs.suricata.io/en/latest/rules/modbus-keyword.html)).

blocks.title: Zeek handles three Modbus requests seen on the SPAN port

scenes.caption: Zeek's Modbus analyzer parses each message on port 502 and raises a modbus_message event with the parsed MBAP header and function code. The script keeps two sets: approved writers and write codes.
Request 1: HMI 10.2.0.10 reads input register 0 (function 4). It is a request, but 4 is not a write code, so the handler returns.
Request 2: the HMI writes HIGH_SP (function 6). It is a write, but the sender is in the writers set: an approved operator change.
Request 3: laptop 10.0.1.20 writes the same register. Every check passes through to NOTICE, which lands in notice.log for the SOC (security operations center).
scenes.output: notice.log  ModbusWatch::Unexpected_Write  Modbus write fc=6 from 10.0.1.20 to 10.3.0.20

blocks.code:
# suricata.yaml: the Modbus parser is disabled by default
app-layer:
  protocols:
    modbus:
      enabled: yes
      detection-ports:
        dp: 502

# rules/ot-local.rules
alert modbus ![10.2.0.10,10.2.0.30] any -> 10.3.0.0/24 502 (msg:"OT Modbus write from unexpected host"; modbus: access write; classtype:policy-violation; sid:9000101; rev:1;)
alert modbus !10.2.0.0/24 any -> 10.3.0.0/24 502 (msg:"OT Modbus from outside the operations zone"; flow:to_server; classtype:policy-violation; sid:9000102; rev:1;)
alert modbus any any -> 10.3.0.0/24 502 (msg:"OT Modbus write to holding register 0 (tank HIGH_SP) above 350"; modbus: access write holding, address 1, value >350; classtype:policy-violation; sid:9000103; rev:1;)
blocks.caption: Rule 1 mirrors the Zeek script. Rule 3 watches the value itself: Suricata's Modbus addresses start at 1, so the docs say add 1 to a zero-based address (register 0 becomes address 1). The sid numbers are local placeholders.

blocks.md: Start every OT monitoring project in learn mode: list every pair of hosts that speak each industrial protocol and every function code they use. That list becomes your allowlist, and the Zeek and Suricata rules above become one-line edits of it.

blocks.question: A consultant proposes an aggressive network scan of all PLCs to build the inventory during production. What does NIST advise?
options: Go ahead: scans are harmless
Prefer passive discovery from SPAN ports or taps; schedule any active scanning during planned outages because probes may destabilise devices
Scan only at night while running
Unplug each PLC and inspect it
blocks.explain: NIST: passive scans add no traffic; active scans 'may cause device instability or interfere with the device process state' and should be scheduled in planned outages.

blocks.question: The Suricata Modbus rules never fire, even in a test with real write traffic. What is the most likely cause?
options: Modbus writes cannot be detected
Suricata needs encryption keys
The sid numbers are too high
The Modbus app-layer parser is disabled by default in suricata.yaml, so 'alert modbus' rules have nothing to match
blocks.explain: Suricata ships with the Modbus parser disabled. Enable it and set detection port 502; its docs also advise unlimited stream reassembly depth for long-lived Modbus connections.

lessons.title: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual

blocks.md:
In IT, the textbook first move is often to pull the network cable. In OT that cable may carry the only view of a hazardous process. NIST SP 800-82r3 asks for "a focused risk assessment on the OT environment" before responding, because physically isolating a system "may not be possible without impacting operational performance or safety".

**Safety first.** The order is: people and the environment, then the equipment and process, then the investigation. The Ukraine alert told utilities to plan for "the assumption that the ICS is actively working counter to the safe operation of the process": the screens may lie (lesson 8), so verify with local gauges and walk-downs.

**Manual operation.** CISA lists "practice and maintain the ability to operate OT systems manually" among its five primary mitigations; NIST lists "transitioning to manual operations" and "manually validate data" among OT response steps, alongside isolating "enterprise from control or control from safety". The Ukrainian utilities restored power this way; Norsk Hydro, a Norwegian aluminium producer hit by LockerGoga ransomware in 2019, "transitioned to manual operations" too (NIST).

blocks.title: A toy OT incident: what each team does in the first hours

scenes.caption: Hour 0: monitoring flags unexpected Modbus writes and an HMI that disagrees with local gauges. First question: is the process safe right now? Operators check with field instruments, not the HMI.

Hour 1: a focused risk assessment decides the response. Here the team moves the tank to manual control (local pump control, walk-downs) before isolating anything, so cutting the network cannot cause a hazard.
Hours 2 to 6: isolate the OT network from IT and, if needed, the control zone from the safety zone; preserve logs and images; compare PLC logic with the offline approved backup.
Hours 6 to 12: restore known-good logic and setpoints, rebuild suspect HMIs from images, return to automatic control step by step. Management notifies regulators and agencies as required.

blocks.md:
**Backups that survive.** NIST: back up "operational data, program files, configuration files, system images, firewall rules, and access control lists", in a "backup-in-depth" design (local, facility and disaster copies, time-sequenced) and test restores. For PLCs, the approved logic and setpoints must be stored offline, because an attacker who changed the controller may also have changed the copy on the engineering workstation (lesson 9).

**Spares and priorities.** NIST suggests stocking hard-to-obtain critical components and prioritising recovery by start-up order: utilities before production.

**Who is in the room.** Control engineers and operators lead on process decisions; the security team leads on evidence and eradication. A plan that skips either fails.

blocks.code:
# ot-incident-runbook.yaml (excerpt for the toy water plant)
trigger: [modbus_write_unexpected, hmi_sensor_mismatch, plc_block_changed]
step_1_safety:
  owner: shift supervisor
  do: confirm tank level with local gauge LG-101 and SIS transmitter LT-201
  if_unsafe: trip pump P-101 locally; call emergency procedure EP-3
step_2_decide:
  owner: control engineer + security lead
  do: focused risk assessment; can we isolate without losing safety or view?
step_3_manual:
  do: switch P-101 to local HAND control; operator stationed at tank
step_4_contain:
  do: [block IT-to-OT conduit, disable vendor VPN accounts, preserve firewall and Zeek logs]
step_5_verify_logic:
  do: export PLC-1 logic with clean laptop; compare with offline golden copy
step_6_restore:
  do: [restore approved logic and setpoints, rebuild HMI-1 from image, return to AUTO in stages]
notify: [management, regulator per sector rules, CISA]
blocks.caption: An illustrative runbook: tag names and procedure numbers are invented. The order mirrors NIST's OT response considerations: safety, decision, manual operation, containment, verification, recovery.

blocks.md: Two IT reflexes can hurt in OT: rebooting or reimaging a running HMI or server (NIST: rebooting 'may not be acceptable'), and running active scans across the control network during an incident. Both can stop the process or the operators' only view of it.
In OT incident response, first make the process safe (using instruments you trust), then keep it running by hand if needed, and only then contain, investigate and restore from offline backups.

blocks.question: During an incident, the security lead wants to disconnect the control network immediately. What should happen first according to NIST's OT guidance?
options: A focused risk assessment with operations: confirm the process is safe and that operators can run it manually or without the network, then isolate
Disconnect immediately; safety is someone else's job
Wait until the next planned outage
Reboot every HMI to clear the infection
blocks.explain: NIST notes isolation may harm operational performance or safety and calls for a focused risk assessment to pick the response. Moving to manual operation first often makes isolation safe.

blocks.question: Why must the 'golden' PLC logic backup be kept offline?
options: Offline storage is faster
An attacker who altered the PLC may also alter or hide changes in online copies and tools, so the reference must be out of reach
PLCs cannot read online backups
Regulators forbid online backups
blocks.explain: Stuxnet hid its blocks from the engineering software. A reference copy that the attacker cannot reach, compared using a clean machine, is the only trustworthy baseline.

lessons.title: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS

blocks.md:
**Regulations and frameworks** turn this course's practices into obligations or checklists:
- **NERC CIP** (North American Electric Reliability Corporation, Critical Infrastructure Protection): mandatory, auditable standards with penalties for the bulk electric system, which NIST describes as generation and high-voltage transmission "above 100 kV". The standards include CIP-002 (categorising systems), CIP-005 (electronic security perimeters), CIP-007 (system security management, including patching), CIP-008 (incident reporting and response), CIP-010 (change management), CIP-013 (supply chain) and the new CIP-015 (internal network security monitoring, not yet enforced). See [NERC's CIP standards](https://www.nerc.com/pa/Stand/Pages/CIPStandards.aspx).
- **ISA/IEC 62443** (lesson 5): voluntary international standards across the lifecycle, from 2-1 (asset owner programs) and 3-2 (risk assessment, zones and conduits) to 3-3 (system security requirements and security levels) and 4-1 and 4-2 (secure product development and component requirements).

- **NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3** (September 2023): the US guide used throughout this course, with an OT overlay for the NIST SP 800-53 control catalogue.
- **CISA guidance**: ICS advisories and alerts, the 2025 primary mitigations and asset inventory guidance, and free training with Idaho National Laboratory.

**MITRE ATT&CK for ICS.** MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is "a globally-accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations". Its [ICS matrix](https://attack.mitre.org/matrices/ics/) has 12 tactics, the attacker's goals: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Evasion, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Command and Control, Inhibit Response Function, Impair Process Control and Impact. Under them sit techniques such as Modify Parameter, Manipulation of View, Program Download, Change Operating Mode and Loss of Safety, each with real procedure examples and mitigations.

Defenders use it to tag alerts (so a report says "Modify Parameter" rather than "weird Modbus thing"), to check which techniques their monitoring covers, and to plan exercises. Technique identifiers do change between versions, so cite names along with IDs.

blocks.title: Cases in this course mapped to ATT&CK for ICS tactics

scenes.caption: 1 means ATT&CK for ICS lists the case under at least one technique of that tactic among those we checked. Stuxnet touches every column: removable media in, program download, rootkit, modified parameters, manipulated view.
Two tactics exist only in the ICS matrix: Inhibit Response Function (stopping safety and protection from working) and Impair Process Control (changing what the process does).
Triton's row: in through remote services, program download to the SIS, a change of operating mode, modified controller firmware, unauthorized command messages, and the impact Loss of Safety.

Unitronics: Internet Accessible Device in, default credentials, denial of service, then loss of view and availability. Simple exposures still cause real outages. Simplified: absence of a 1 means not listed in our check, not proven absent.

# Tag each alert from this course's detectors with ATT&CK for ICS
# technique names (and tactic), so reports speak one language.
ATTACK = {
    "modbus_write_unexpected": ("Modify Parameter", "Impair Process Control"),
    "hmi_sensor_mismatch":     ("Manipulation of View", "Impact"),
    "plc_block_changed":       ("Modify Program", "Persistence"),
    "remote_vpn_unapproved":   ("External Remote Services", "Initial Access"),
    "sis_key_in_program":      ("Change Operating Mode", "Execution, Evasion"),
    "ot_port_on_internet":     ("Internet Accessible Device", "Initial Access"),
}
alerts = ["remote_vpn_unapproved", "modbus_write_unexpected", "hmi_sensor_mismatch"]

for a in alerts:
    technique, tactic = ATTACK[a]
    print(f"{a:26} {technique:26} [{tactic}]")
blocks.caption: Runnable Python. Output: the VPN alert maps to External Remote Services [Initial Access], the Modbus write to Modify Parameter [Impair Process Control], the sensor mismatch to Manipulation of View [Impact]. Tactics checked against each technique page.

**Practise legally.** Industrial equipment is the one place where a careless test can hurt someone: never scan, probe or connect to equipment you do not own or have written permission to test.
- [CISA ICS training](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/programs/ics-training-available-through-cisa) with Idaho National Laboratory: self-paced online courses through the [Virtual Learning Portal](https://ics-training.inl.gov/).
- Public ICS packet captures to analyse offline: the [4SICS ICS lab captures](https://www.netresec.com/?page=PCAP4SICS) from Netresec, and [Wireshark's sample captures](https://wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures), which include Modbus. Run the parser from lesson 6 and the Zeek script from lesson 14 on them.
- [try.zeek.org](https://try.zeek.org/) to run Zeek scripts in the browser.

Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

blocks.question: A utility runs a 200 kV transmission substation in the United States. Which set of rules is mandatory for its cyber security, with audits and penalties?
options: ISA/IEC 62443, because it is international
NIST SP 800-82, because it is from the US government
MITRE ATT&CK for ICS
NERC CIP standards for the bulk electric system
blocks.explain: NERC CIP applies to bulk electric systems (NIST: above 100 kV) and includes audit measures and penalties. IEC 62443 and NIST SP 800-82 are guidance; ATT&CK is a knowledge base, not a rule set.

blocks.question: An intruder raises the high-level alarm threshold on the HMI so operators are never warned. Which ATT&CK for ICS tactic is this?
options: Collection
Discovery
Inhibit Response Function
Command and Control
blocks.explain: MITRE: in Inhibit Response Function 'the adversary is trying to prevent your safety, protection, quality assurance, and operator intervention functions from responding'. Modify Alarm Settings and Alarm Suppression are techniques under it.
